cardyiq.name: Cardy
cardyiq.tagline: A live product, a backend rebuild, a new business model, and a team of ten. Engineering goes beyond the code.
cardyiq.summary: I rebuilt Cardyiq while it was live. It grew from a broken launch to 150+ venues in 6 cities with 99.9% uptime.
cardyiq.role: Founding Engineer & Technical Lead · manages a team of 10
stack: Redis (cache + ops: queues, locks, rate limits, idempotency)

sections.heading: Context
sections.lede: The product was live. It was not ready.
sections.body:
Cardyiq is a sports and fitness network in Iraq. I was asked to give some "technical advice" a few days after launch. The app was live, people were already using it and almost every part underneath needed work.

I cannot publish the operational details, but I can show what was wrong, what I changed and what happened after.

sections.heading: What I inherited
bullets: It failed on Iraqi networks. A DNS/CDN problem made the app unreachable for many users. The old advice was to install a VPN.
The Laravel/MySQL backend was fragile. Small changes were risky and slow.
There was no CI/CD and no caching. Deploying was painful, so it rarely happened.
Payments were cash only. Someone had to collect the money from every venue.
The dashboard was in English. The people using it every day spoke Arabic.
The business model was the biggest problem. Entry passes limited the sports, venues and pricing the product could support.

sections.heading: My ownership
bullets: I stabilised the Laravel/MySQL backend while users were still inside the app.
I rebuilt the dashboard in React and made it Arabic-first.
I kept the Flutter app shipping during the rebuild.
I built delivery with Docker, GitHub Actions and Dokploy. We shipped 30 releases in 6 months.
I moved the product to hosting that Iraqi networks could reach reliably.
I integrated two payment providers behind one idempotent, webhook-reconciled layer.
I added backups, a read replica and a recovery path before the incident happened.
I replaced entry passes with points and subscriptions.
I built and now manage the 10-person team that runs it with me.

sections.heading: System map
sections.diagram:
USER  ──▶ MOBILE APP (Flutter) ──────────────┐
OWNER ──▶ DASHBOARD (React · Arabic-first) ──┤
                                             ▼
                                       API (Bun · Express · TypeScript)
                                             │
                                             ▼
                                       PostgreSQL primary ──▶ read replica + backups (the recovery path)

PAYMENTS  provider A ─┐
          provider B ─┴─▶ webhook reconciliation
                                    │
                                    ▼
                     initiated → pending → confirmed
                                    │
                                    ├──▶ failed  (explicit state, never guessed)
                                    └──▶ retry   (idempotent, no double charge)

DELIVERY  git push ─▶ GitHub Actions ─▶ Docker build ─▶ Dokploy ─▶ zero-downtime deploy

items.title: Fix the business model before polishing the code.
items.text: Entry passes put a ceiling on the product. Points and subscriptions opened it to more sports and more kinds of venues. Without that change, the technical rebuild would not matter.

items.title: Keep the product live.
items.text: There was no downtime window. I moved the hosting, changed the database and rebuilt features in small steps under live traffic.

items.title: Kill cash with one abstraction.
items.text: Both providers sit behind one idempotent, webhook-reconciled layer. The app does not need to know which provider is handling the payment.

items.title: Recovery paths before features.
items.text: The backups and read replica existed before the incident. That was the reason we recovered without losing a record.

items.title: Hire the team that makes you unnecessary.
items.text: I built a team of 10 and gave people enough context and ownership to move without waiting for me.

sections.heading: Outcome
sections.body: The 99.9% uptime does not mean nothing went wrong. We had a production data incident and recovered with zero records lost. The next section explains it.

sections.heading: The incident room
sections.body:
A data-loss incident was detected in production. Here is the public version of what happened.

The incident was bad. The good part was that the recovery path already existed and we did not lose anyone's data.

items.title: We found the issue
items.text: Monitoring showed something was wrong in the primary database. The app stayed online while we checked the damage.

items.title: We checked the replica
items.text: The read replica was intact and consistent.

items.title: We checked the backups
items.text: We compared the backup timeline with the replica and confirmed exactly what was affected.

items.title: We chose the recovery path
items.text: The replica became the source of truth. The backups were used to verify it.

items.title: We verified everything
items.text: We checked the data against both sources before returning to normal operation.

items.title: Zero records lost
items.text: The recovery setup worked exactly when we needed it.

sections.quote: The incident was bad. The good part was that the recovery path already existed and we did not lose anyone's data.

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.body: The code was only part of the problem. Operations and the business model needed work too.

sections.heading: What I'd change today
sections.body: I would build the payment layer and observability in week one, not month two. I would also push the business-model conversation earlier. The code was not the hardest part. Getting everyone to agree that entry passes were the ceiling took longer.

qi-card.name: Qi
qi-card.tagline: Tasdid and Jabi, plus oil stations, AML, Qi Hawala, service providers, KRG billing, Basmayah loans, and native mini-app work.
qi-card.summary: Engineering across Qi: Tasdid, Jabi, oil stations, AML dashboards, service-provider mini-apps, Qi Hawala, KRG / e-Psule, Bismayah, and native DSL.
stack: AXML · ACSS · JavaScript (native DSL mini program)

stats.label: users of the billing & merchant products
native Jabi+ port alongside H5 mini-app work

sections.heading: Context
sections.lede: My work at Qi reaches across products people use and the tools that keep operations running.
sections.body:
I work across Tasdid, Jabi, oil stations, AML dashboards, service-provider mini-apps, Qi Hawala, KRG / e-Psule, Bismayah, and native DSL. Some of that work lives inside SuperQi’s Alipay mini-app ecosystem. Some lives in operational web applications.

Tasdid and Jabi are the two projects I highlight here. The full collection below includes the other products and systems I’ve worked on at Qi.

sections.heading: Billing constraints
bullets: The product had to feel obvious to normal people, often over 50 and using it for the first time.
It still had to work on low-end Android phones and unreliable networks.
Multiple bill providers with wildly different response times and failure behaviours.
The UI can have a visual bug. It can never guess what happened to someone's money.
Hard bundle-size budgets inside the super-app runtime.
Every flow passes internal security review; payments run on wallet and tokenization-supported card rails.
Kurdish, Arabic and English had to work from the start, including right-to-left layouts.

sections.heading: Billing & merchant work
bullets: I designed and built the Svelte/SvelteKit frontend architecture inside the Alipay mini-app runtime.
I built bill inquiry, invoices, payment selection and provider-specific error states.
I added caching and progressive loading so the useful parts show up first.
I integrated wallet and tokenization-supported card payments through security review.
I shipped filtering, sorting, pagination and Excel export for Jabi+.
I delivered e-Psule in Kurdish, Arabic and English.

sections.heading: Billing flow
sections.body: One representative flow from the billing mini-app work.
sections.diagram:
USER ──▶ TASDID+ (Svelte mini-app) ──▶ SuperQi / Alipay runtime ──▶ Billing APIs
              │                                             │
              │  cache · progressive loading                ├──▶ provider A  (fast)
              │  skeleton → partial → complete              ├──▶ provider B  (slow)
              ▼                                             └──▶ provider N  (flaky)
        invoice normalized
              │
              ▼
   payment method (wallet · tokenized card)
              │
              ▼
   TRANSACTION STATE MACHINE
   initiated → pending → authorized → confirmed
                 │
                 ├──▶ failed   (provider-specific message)
                 └──▶ retry    (no double-charge: idempotent)

items.title: Separate UI state from transaction state.
items.text: The app can crash, reload or lose the network and still recover. It never invents a payment result. The state machine owns that truth.

items.title: Svelte for the phones people actually own.
items.text: Svelte gave us a small bundle and fast cold start. That mattered more than framework preference.

items.title: Progressive loading over spinners.
items.text: Providers answer at different speeds. The screen fills in as responses arrive instead of waiting for the slowest one.

items.title: Provider errors stay distinct.
items.text: A timeout, invalid account and provider outage are different problems. The user gets a useful message for each one.

items.title: Merchant tools don't assume a laptop.
items.text: For many merchants, the phone is the whole back office. Jabi+ keeps large datasets usable on a small screen and still exports to Excel when the accountant needs it.

sections.heading: Outcome
sections.body: Independently retained by five startups to integrate the same payment rails.

items.title: Provider timeout
items.text: Distinct state with its own copy and retry path; the rest of the screen keeps working.

items.title: Payment pending
items.text: The UI says pending. It never guesses success. The final answer comes from the source of truth.

items.title: User cancels mid-flow
items.text: Transaction state machine unwinds cleanly; no orphaned intents.

items.title: Slow network
items.text: Cache serves the last known state instantly; the network upgrades it when it can.

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.body: Payments are better when they are boring. Clear states, small bundles and careful reviews make that possible.

sections.heading: What I'd change today
sections.body: I would define a shared latency budget for every provider before product design starts. Then each new mini-app would inherit the same progressive-loading behaviour instead of deciding it again.

asheerty.name: Asheerty
asheerty.tagline: Old family material becomes a living tree, then a piece of art for the wall. I’m building the whole journey.
asheerty.summary: Build a family tree in the app, then print, frame and deliver it. Built solo and live on iOS and Android.
stack: Claude Code and Codex used as build tools

stats.label: app stores · live on iOS + Android
full pipeline: app → framed artwork → delivery, operating

sections.heading: Context
sections.lede: Many families still keep their tree on paper in one person's drawer.
sections.body:
Asheerty lets them build the tree in a mobile app. The tree becomes a painting that is printed, framed and delivered.

It is not a PDF export. It is a real object the family can hang on the wall.

sections.heading: The constraints
bullets: Family trees are irregular. Generations, marriages and large branches still need to produce a balanced print.
The artwork is physical: errors cost real money in print and shipping, so human review must gate production.
I built the iOS app, Android app, dashboard, backend and fulfilment flow while working two other jobs.
Cultural gravity: names, order and lineage must be treated with respect. Families will hang this on a wall.

sections.heading: My ownership
bullets: I designed and built everything solo, using Claude Code and Codex where they helped.
I built the React Native editor for members, branches, relationships, generations and preview.
I built the React dashboard for review, layout correction, approval and print readiness.
I implemented the Bun and Express backend.
I built the AI-assisted recognition flow that helps find faces, read names and suggest relationships from family material.
I built the generation flow that turns the reviewed family tree into organic, family-specific artwork ready for print.
I built the order flow from submission to a framed print at the door.

sections.heading: System map
sections.diagram:
FAMILY MATERIAL (photos · names · documents)
      │
      ▼
AI RECOGNITION (faces · names · possible relationships)
      │
      ▼
HUMAN REVIEW (check · correct · approve)
      │
      ▼
FAMILY DATABASE ──▶ INTERACTIVE TREE (mobile app)
      │
      ▼
AI ARTWORK PIPELINE (layout · organic composition · generation · refinement)
      │
      ▼
FINAL REVIEW ──▶ PRINT PREPARATION ──▶ PHYSICAL ARTWORK ──▶ DELIVERY

items.title: The artwork is the product. The app is how you make it.
items.text: Every technical choice serves the final framed print. The app exists so a family can get the tree onto their wall, not the other way around.

items.title: Human review before ink.
items.text: A dashboard step catches layout problems while they're still pixels. Once ink touches paper, a mistake costs money, shipping time, and a family's trust.

items.title: AI helps at both ends. People still approve the truth.
items.text: AI helps read the original material and create the final artwork. Family relationships and the piece sent to print still pass through human review.

items.title: Ship early, say so.
items.text: It launched recently and has under 100 users. I am saying that plainly. It is still live on both app stores with physical fulfilment, and I built it solo.

items.title: Unbalanced tree layout
items.text: The review dashboard flags and corrects it before print.

items.title: Order stuck between states
items.text: Explicit order-state machine with operational visibility.

items.title: Reprint requests
items.text: The approved final artwork is stored so the exact piece can be printed again.

items.title: Data entry mistakes
items.text: Preview + review loop before anything physical happens.

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.body: A bug on screen is annoying. A bug that gets printed, framed and shipped costs real money.

sections.heading: What I'd change today
sections.body: I would test printers, colour, paper and sizes earlier. I would also build a shareable preview so the whole family can check the tree before someone orders it.

notifyx.name: NotifyX
notifyx.tagline: I kept rebuilding notifications. So I made one system for providers, retries, scheduling, and delivery states.
notifyx.summary: One notification API for four push providers. Open source, used by five companies and benchmarked at about 150 messages per second per worker.
stack: Providers: FCM, APNS, HMS, Web Push

stats.label: campaigns to 10K+ users at Cardyiq alone

sections.heading: Context
sections.lede: I was tired of solving the same problem inside every product.
sections.body:
Every app needed push notifications, scheduling, retries and delivery state. I kept rebuilding it. NotifyX is the version I can reuse everywhere.

It puts FCM, APNS, HMS and Web Push behind one API. The caller sends a message. NotifyX handles providers, queues, retries and delivery state. The code is public at github.com/awsdang/notifyx.

sections.heading: The constraints
bullets: Four providers have different tokens, limits and failure behaviour. The caller should not care.
Messages must never be silently lost: every message ends in an accountable state.
Scheduled and immediate delivery through the same pipeline.
Several products and companies share one deployment, so multi-tenancy existed from the start.
Operations people need visibility without reading logs.
A worker crash must not lose queued work. Ever.

sections.heading: My ownership
bullets: I built the API, workers and scheduler with Node.js, BullMQ, Redis, PostgreSQL and Prisma.
I added retries with backoff and a dead-letter queue for permanent failures.
I built the React dashboard so delivery state is visible without searching logs.
I wrote SDKs for web, Flutter and React Native.
I benchmarked and tuned it to about 150 messages per second per worker.

sections.heading: System map
sections.diagram:
API ─────────┐   (immediate)
SCHEDULER ───┤   (timed campaigns)
             ▼
      QUEUE · BullMQ / Redis          (the source of truth)
             │
             ▼
      WORKERS 1..N                    (disposable · ~150 msg/s each)
             │
             ├──▶ FCM         (Android)
             ├──▶ APNS        (iOS)
             ├──▶ HMS         (Huawei)
             └──▶ WEB PUSH    (browsers)
             │
           failed
             ├──▶ RETRY (backoff) ──▶ back to the queue
             └──▶ DEAD-LETTER         (permanent · kept for human inspection)
             │
      delivery state ──▶ PostgreSQL ──▶ REACT DASHBOARD

items.title: One API, four providers.
items.text: Token formats, payloads and rate limits belong inside the adapters. The caller only needs to say "send this."

items.title: The queue is the source of truth.
items.text: Workers are disposable. If one dies in the middle of a batch, BullMQ gives the job to another worker. The crash loses nothing.

items.title: Failures are data.
items.text: Invalid tokens are removed, timeouts retry with backoff and permanent failures go to a dead-letter lane a person can inspect.

items.title: Stable device identity.
items.text: The web SDK anchors devices to a client-managed external ID, so push-subscription rotations update one device record instead of creating ghosts.

sections.heading: Outcome
sections.body: Cardyiq, Sadeek, Asheerty, Orivo and Baseerah use NotifyX. It is now the default notification layer for the products I ship.

items.title: Provider timeout
items.text: Retry with backoff; delivery state preserved through every attempt.

items.title: Invalid token
items.text: The dead token is removed so we do not keep sending to it.

items.title: Provider rate limit
items.text: The queue absorbs the burst; workers pace the drain.

items.title: Worker crash
items.text: BullMQ re-delivers the job to a healthy worker. No message lost.

items.title: Permanent failure
items.text: Dead-letter lane with full context, waiting for a human.

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.body: The success path is easy. I trust infrastructure when I know exactly what it does after something fails.

sections.heading: What I'd change today
sections.body: I would add per-tenant rate-limit budgets earlier so one company cannot slow down another. I would also define delivery receipts properly from the start. And I would open-source it on day one instead of extracting the public version later.

sadeek.name: Sadeek
sadeek.tagline: Send a photo through Telegram. Get a cleaned image, a description, a suggested price, and tools inside the conversation.
sadeek.summary: A Telegram AI product built around photos, image tools, content generation, and stateful conversations. 10K+ users and 150K+ AI requests.
stack: Newer backend: grammY, Bun/Express, PostgreSQL, Redis, BullMQ

sections.heading: Context
sections.lede: Merchants had one rough phone photo, no laptop and products they wanted to sell.
sections.body:
They already used Telegram, so I built Sadeek there. A merchant sent a photo. Sadeek cleaned it, wrote the description, suggested a price, checked the listing and published it to sadeek.app.

It reached 10K+ users, handled 150K+ AI requests, drew 40K monthly visitors and made usage-based revenue. I built and operated the whole thing alone.

sections.heading: The constraints
bullets: The whole product had to fit inside a Telegram conversation.
Cost per AI request had to stay under what usage-based pricing could recover, or every new user was a loss.
The input was usually one bad phone photo, but the output still had to look sellable.
A stateful conversation bot at 10K-user scale: every merchant is mid-flow somewhere, and the bot must remember where.
Generated listings needed moderation before real buyers could see them.
Model APIs fail, change behaviour and change price. The pipeline had to handle all three.

sections.heading: My ownership
bullets: I built the product, architecture, code and operations alone.
I built the Telegram flow from the first photo to the published listing.
I built the n8n pipeline with stages, retries and fallbacks.
I used GPT and Gemini for descriptions, pricing and moderation.
I shipped background removal, relighting and AI try-on.
I ran PostgreSQL, the Next.js storefront and usage-based billing.

sections.heading: System map
sections.diagram:
MERCHANT ──▶ TELEGRAM BOT  (one photo · a few words · nothing to install)
                  │
                  ▼
         n8n ORCHESTRATION  stateful conversation · cost-aware routing
                  │
         ┌────────┴─────────────────┐   (in parallel)
         ▼                          ▼
   IMAGE PIPELINE             LLM CONTENT
   bg removal · relight       description · pricing
   AI try-on                  (GPT + Gemini)
         │                          │
         │   model API down ──▶ fallback lane: alternate provider · retry
         └────────┬─────────────────┘
                  ▼
         MODERATION GATE  nothing publishes unreviewed
                  ▼
         PostgreSQL / API
                  ▼
         NEXT.JS STOREFRONT ──▶ listing live  (auto-published)

items.title: Telegram as the entire onboarding.
items.text: Merchants already trusted Telegram. There was no download, signup form or laptop. They could start where they already were.

items.title: AI cost is an architecture concern.
items.text: Batching, model routing and caching decided whether the product could make money. Clever prompts were not enough.

items.title: A pipeline, not a prompt.
items.text: Quality came from staged processing with checks between stages, not from one giant model call. Each stage could be measured, retried, and improved independently.

items.title: Hide the models.
items.text: Merchants saw "photo in, listing out." Provider names, API failures, and fallback switches stayed backstage, handled operationally. Nobody selling shoes cares which model relit the photo.

items.title: Moderate before publish.
items.text: Every listing passed moderation before buyers saw it. That stage never had a shortcut.

sections.heading: Outcome
sections.body: The hard parts were cost per request, image quality from bad inputs and keeping the bot in the right state for thousands of users. The model was not the hard part.

sections.heading: The product question
sections.body:
The interesting question was whether Sadeek should stay a tool for individual merchants or become infrastructure that other commerce platforms could use.

Those are two different products. One needs a simple daily workflow. The other needs APIs, integrations and strong operational guarantees.

If I took it further, I would choose merchant infrastructure and build around that decision from day one.
sections.quote: If I took it further, I would choose merchant infrastructure and build around that decision from day one.

sections.heading: Telegram is the product
sections.lede: Send a photo. Stay in the conversation.
sections.body: The bot, conversation state, image tools, content generation, and usage controls are the core of Sadeek. The store is a secondary publishing surface.

items.title: A phone photo
items.text: The merchant starts inside Telegram. Onboarding and saved preferences provide context for the request.

items.title: Image + content
items.text: The original pipeline combines image cleanup, descriptions, pricing, and moderation with retries and provider fallbacks.

items.title: A stateful conversation
items.text: Callbacks, request history, usage balance, referrals, and subscription flows keep the product inside the chat.

items.title: The conversation has a backend.
items.text: The newer backend uses grammY, Bun/Express, PostgreSQL, Redis, and BullMQ. Its source separates onboarding, photos, callbacks, payments, referrals, search, and admin commands.

items.title: Original pipeline → newer queue branch
items.text: The production story above describes the original n8n workflow. The newer photo handler enqueues work and acknowledges receipt; its final asynchronous Telegram delivery is still marked unfinished in that branch.

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.body: In a real AI product, cost, quality and failure handling matter more than the demo.

sections.heading: What I'd change today
sections.body: I would choose one product from day one: merchant infrastructure. I would charge earlier because free users taught me about growth, not willingness to pay. I would also set a cost budget for every request before building the pipeline.

hawsr.name: HAWSR
hawsr.tagline: A master’s thesis became my first company. Building models in a browser, real customers, and a lot of firsts.
hawsr.summary: My master's thesis became a construction-tech company. It built 3D web tools, made about $60K and was later shut down.

sections.heading: Context
sections.lede: Most theses become PDFs. I tried to turn mine into a business.
sections.body:
I worked as an architect for nine years, including reconstruction work with UNOPS in Anbar. After teaching myself to code, my thesis automated the delivery of Revit building models to the web. I turned that idea into HAWSR.

The company did not last, but it gave me my first serious product, customers, revenue and a team of six to lead. It was the point where software became my career.

sections.heading: The constraints
bullets: BIM models are huge. They needed heavy optimisation before they could load on a normal laptop.
The Revit to web step had to be automated. Manual export did not scale.
Iraqi construction clients had never bought software like this. Every sale started with explaining that the category existed.
Funding was limited, so revenue had to carry the company.
I was learning engineering, sales and product at the same time while paying clients watched.

sections.heading: My ownership
bullets: I built the Three.js and React platform for exploring building models in a browser.
I automated the Revit to web pipeline with Dynamo and Python.
I researched converting 360° captures into Gaussian Splatting scenes.
I won first prize at The Station Foundation incubator.
I presented the product to an audience of more than 1,000 people.
I sold and delivered about $60K of work.
I built and led a team of six while learning product, sales and engineering.

sections.heading: System map
sections.diagram:
REVIT MODEL
     │
     ▼
DYNAMO + PYTHON automation  (no manual export · the pipeline runs itself)
     │
     ▼
optimized geometry  (BIM-scale models, browser-scale payloads)
     │
     ▼
THREE.JS / R3F WEB VIEWER
     │
     ▼
client browser  (no install · no plugin · a link)

R&D LANE (experimental)
360° CAPTURE ──▶ processing (Insta360 SDK) ──▶ GAUSSIAN SPLATTING scene

items.title: Product over paper.
items.text: I wanted customers to test the idea, not just a committee. Building the product gave me much better answers.

items.title: Automate the pipeline first.
items.text: The viewer was the demo. The useful part was the Revit to web automation that saved people from doing exports by hand.

items.title: Charge real money early.
items.text: About $60K of revenue proved that some clients would pay. It did not prove the market was big enough.

items.title: Decommission deliberately.
items.text: The market was small, funding was gone and the splat quality was not ready. I chose to shut the company down instead of keeping it half alive.

sections.heading: Outcome
sections.body: HAWSR taught me Three.js, React Three Fiber, automation and product thinking. I still use those skills today, including on this website.

sections.heading: How the run ended
sections.body:
The market was too small. There were construction firms willing to pay, but not enough to grow the company. Funding was gone. Gaussian splatting from 360° capture was also not good enough yet to sell as a product.

Together, those problems were the answer. I handed off the clients, archived the pipeline and shut HAWSR down.

HAWSR did not become the company I wanted. It did turn automation into my software career.
sections.quote: HAWSR did not become the company I wanted. It did turn automation into my software career.

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.body: Technical feasibility, product, and market size are three different questions. I learned to ask all three before writing code.

sections.heading: What I'd change today
sections.body: I would validate the market size before building the full platform. I would sell the automation as a service first and let revenue prove the pipeline. I would also keep splatting as research until the quality was ready.

maaahr.name: Maaahr
maaahr.tagline: A voice interviewer that listens, follows up, and produces a structured evaluation. An exercise in making AI feel less robotic.
maaahr.summary: An HRTech hackathon prototype for voice interview practice with realtime audio, subtitles and structured feedback.

sections.heading: Context
sections.lede: Reading interview advice is not the same as saying the answer out loud.
sections.body: Maaahr started as a text-based AI Engineering capstone. During a hackathon, I rebuilt it on the OpenAI Realtime API. The prototype speaks, listens, shows subtitles and gives a structured report after the interview.

sections.heading: The constraints
bullets: Voice latency has to feel natural. Long silence makes the whole thing awkward.
Barge-in must work: when the user interrupts the interviewer, the interviewer stops.
Voice, transcript and scoring have to stay in sync.
Evaluation must be structured and useful, not vibes.
A product interview and an engineering interview need different questions.

sections.heading: My ownership
bullets: I built the whole product end to end.
I built role-specific question planning so the interview matches the job.
I implemented realtime voice sessions on the OpenAI Realtime API.
I built live transcription and subtitles synced to audio.
I built the evaluation pipeline and reports with GPT and Gemini.

sections.heading: System map
sections.diagram:
ROLE PROFILE ──▶ QUESTION PLANNER
                       │
                       ▼
        REALTIME VOICE SESSION (OpenAI Realtime API)
        listening ⇄ thinking ⇄ speaking ⇄ interrupted
                       │
                       ├──▶ live subtitles   (latency-critical path)
                       └──▶ transcript
                              │
                              ▼
              EVALUATION PIPELINE
              relevance · clarity · completeness
              technical depth · communication
              missed opportunities
                              │
                              ▼
              STRUCTURED FEEDBACK REPORT

items.title: Voice state is a state machine.
items.text: Listening, thinking, speaking and interrupted are explicit states. Interruption is normal because people interrupt.

items.title: Subtitles are trust.
items.text: The live transcript shows the user that the system heard them. It also makes unavoidable latency feel less empty.

items.title: Evaluate against a rubric, not a feeling.
items.text: The report covers relevance, clarity, completeness, technical depth, communication and missed opportunities. That is more useful than saying "good job."

items.title: Product evolution over rewrite.
items.text: The text version's question planner and evaluators moved into the voice version without a rewrite. Only the interaction layer changed.

sections.heading: Outcome
sections.body: The hard parts were latency, interruption and keeping the voice, transcript and score together.

items.title: Realtime session drops
items.text: Graceful reconnect; the transcript is preserved and the interview resumes where it stopped.

items.title: User silence
items.text: The interviewer gives a short prompt instead of hanging forever.

items.title: Transcript drift
items.text: Periodic re-sync between audio and text keeps subtitles honest about what was actually said.

items.title: Model latency spike
items.text: Filler acknowledgements keep the conversational rhythm while the real response is on its way.

sections.heading: What I learned
sections.body: Voice latency cannot be hidden. The product has to make it feel natural.

sections.heading: What I'd change today
sections.body: I would add record and review so users can hear their answer next to the feedback. I would also add different interviewer styles and calibrate the scoring against real hiring decisions.

before-code.name: Before code

before-code.summary: For nine years, I worked in architecture and construction. With UNOPS in Anbar, I managed a reconstruction program covering around 1,500 homes.
